lead: No natural product has strong evidence in alopecia areata. In a 7-month randomized trial in 86 people, a blend of thyme, rosemary, lavender and cedarwood oils massaged into the scalp improved hair loss more often than carrier oil alone (44% vs 15%; grade B), and vitamin D injected into or applied to bald patches has small trials (grade B), but no trials of oral vitamin D supplements were found. Oral zinc is not supported by a systematic review of trials (grade Insufficient), and compounds sold as natural JAK inhibitors, such as quercetin and EGCG, have only laboratory and animal data (grade D).

grade_key.A: Meta-analysis, or at least 2 randomized trials with low risk of bias and a consistent benefit
grade_key.B: 1 good randomized trial, or several randomized trials with mixed results
grade_key.C: Observational studies, small pilots or open-label trials only
grade_key.Negative: Randomized trials found no benefit over placebo

disclaimer: This page summarizes published research. It is not medical advice. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

products.name: Essential oil blend (thyme, rosemary, lavender, cedarwood)
products.summary: In a 7-month double-blind randomized trial in 86 people with alopecia areata, one group massaged a blend of thyme, rosemary, lavender and cedarwood oils in carrier oils into the scalp each day, and the other used carrier oils alone. Improvement was seen in 19 of 43 people (44%) with the essential oils and 6 of 41 (15%) with carrier oil. Because a four-oil blend was tested, the result cannot be attributed to rosemary or any single oil. Trials of rosemary oil in pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) are a different condition and are not counted here. A systematic review of complementary therapies listed this blend among those with the best evidence for hair growth in alopecia areata.
products.safety_interactions: The trial authors described the treatment as safe, but the abstract does not list adverse events. The systematic review found adverse events rare and mild for all the complementary therapies it evaluated. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

products.name: Vitamin D (injected or applied to the scalp)
products.summary: All the treatment studies found used vitamin D3 injected into bald patches or calcipotriol, a vitamin D analogue applied to the scalp; no randomized trials of oral vitamin D supplements in alopecia areata were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026, and the authors of a planned 2022 systematic review said there is no conclusive evidence for supplementation. In a randomized trial in 60 adults with patchy alopecia areata, up to 3 injections of vitamin D3 gave more improvement than saline injections. In a 3-month randomized trial in 60 people, scalp severity scores improved from baseline with calcipotriol, ultraviolet B light, or both, but not with placebo. A 2026 meta-analysis found benefit for injected vitamin D3, an uncertain effect for topical vitamin D3 (the confidence interval crossed zero), and lower efficacy for injected vitamin D3 than for injected corticosteroid, based on a small number of trials. Separately, a meta-analysis of 14 observational studies found lower blood vitamin D levels in people with alopecia areata than in controls; that is an association, not evidence that supplements help.
products.safety_interactions: The injection trial reported negligible, short-lived side effects, and the meta-analysis found no serious adverse events with vitamin D3 or its analogues. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

products.name: Curcumin (in a topical mix with piperine and capsaicin)
products.summary: In a 3-month randomized trial in 60 people, a scalp preparation combining piperine, capsaicin and curcumin was compared with 5% minoxidil, with no placebo group. Both groups had regrowth (effective in 63% with the mix and 70% with minoxidil), and the mix was not shown to be better than minoxidil. Because three ingredients were combined and there was no placebo, the trial cannot show what curcumin itself does, and it is not evidence that curcumin blocks JAK enzymes in people. No trials of oral curcumin or turmeric in alopecia areata were found.
products.safety_interactions: Side effects were temporary and no serious adverse events occurred in the trial. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited trial.

citations.label: Mao et al., 2022, J Cosmet Dermatol
citations.title: Efficacy of a mixed preparation containing piperine, capsaicin and curcumin in the treatment of alopecia areata.

products.name: Garlic gel (topical, added to a steroid cream)
products.summary: In a 3-month double-blind randomized trial in 40 people with localized alopecia areata, everyone used a corticosteroid cream (betamethasone), and half also applied garlic gel while half applied a placebo gel. A good response was reported in 19 of 20 people in the garlic group, which the authors reported as significantly better than the control group; the abstract does not give the control group's response rate. Graded C because it is one small add-on trial.
products.safety_interactions: The trial reported no complications. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited trial.

general_safety.name: Garlic
general_safety.short: Case reports of altered platelet function and clotting, with possible bleeding risk, and of burns from raw garlic on skin. May enhance warfarin; lowered saquinavir levels in a study.

citations.label: Hajheydari et al., 2007, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol
citations.title: Combination of topical garlic gel and betamethasone valerate cream in the treatment of localized alopecia areata: a double-blind randomized controlled study.

products.name: Onion juice (topical)
products.summary: In a small controlled study that did not report randomization, 23 people with patchy alopecia areata applied crude onion juice to the scalp twice a day and 15 applied tap water, for two months. Regrowth was seen in 20 of the onion-juice group (87%) at six weeks and in 2 of the tap-water group (13%) at eight weeks. The groups were unequal in size and were assessed at different time points.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

citations.label: Sharquie et al., 2002, J Dermatol
citations.title: Onion juice (Allium cepa L.), a new topical treatment for alopecia areata.

products.name: Total glucosides of paeony
products.summary: Two randomized trials from one Chinese group had no placebo group. In 86 adults with mild to moderate alopecia areata, paeony glucoside capsules and compound glycyrrhizin tablets, another plant-derived product, gave similar response rates after 3 months. In 117 children with severe alopecia areata, adding paeony glucosides to glycyrrhizin tablets gave lower severity scores than glycyrrhizin alone, and better response rates at 6 and 12 months.
products.safety_interactions: Adverse reactions were reported in 6 of 44 adults taking paeony glucosides and 7 of 42 taking glycyrrhizin tablets, a similar rate. In the children's trial, adverse event rates did not differ and no severe adverse events were observed. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Total glucosides of paeony
general_safety.short: Trials report diarrhoea or stomach discomfort as the commonest side effects, with no severe events; added to standard drugs it did not raise adverse reactions.

products.name: Green tea catechin EGCG
products.summary: EGCG is also marketed as a natural JAK inhibitor. The only alopecia areata study found treated cell lines and blood immune cells from patients in the laboratory; it suggested EGCG lowered JAK2 expression in those cells. No studies of people taking or applying EGCG for alopecia areata were found.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials, because no human treatment studies were found.

general_safety.name: Green tea extract and EGCG
general_safety.short: Concentrated green tea extracts taken in large doses, especially when fasting, have been linked to liver injury in case reports and trials; brewed tea was not.

citations.label: Hamed et al., 2018, Int J Environ Res Public Health
citations.title: Epigallocatechin-3 Gallate Inhibits STAT-1/JAK2/IRF-1/HLA-DR/HLA-B and Reduces CD8 MKG2D Lymphocytes of Alopecia Areata Patients.

products.name: Quercetin
products.summary: Quercetin is often listed as a natural JAK inhibitor, but the only alopecia areata study found was in mice: hair regrew in mice with alopecia areata given quercetin injections under the skin, and not in sham-treated mice. No human studies were found. Approved JAK inhibitor medicines are a different thing: baricitinib, the first JAK inhibitor approved for severe alopecia areata in the USA and EU, was tested in two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in people. Laboratory findings for quercetin do not show it works like these medicines.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials, because no human studies of quercetin in alopecia areata were found.

general_safety.name: Quercetin
general_safety.short: Human studies report rare, mild side effects; long-term high-dose safety is unknown. May alter levels of some drugs (CYP2C9, CYP2E1 and P-glycoprotein substrates).

citations.title: Prevention and treatment of alopecia areata with quercetin in the C3H/HeJ mouse model.

citations.label: Fung et al., 2023, Am J Clin Dermatol
citations.title: Baricitinib: A Review in Severe Alopecia Areata.

products.name: Resveratrol
products.summary: No randomized, observational, pilot or laboratory studies of resveratrol in alopecia areata were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026. Claims that it acts as a natural JAK inhibitor for hair loss rest on research in other conditions.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials, because no alopecia areata studies were found.

general_safety.name: Resveratrol
general_safety.short: Generally well tolerated up to 1 g/day; 2.5 to 5 g/day caused mild to moderate gut symptoms. Changes CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and CYP1A2 activity, so may interact with medicines.

products.name: Zinc (oral)
products.summary: A systematic review of randomized trials of systemic treatments for alopecia areata concluded that the evidence does not support oral zinc sulphate; it does not report trials showing no benefit over placebo, so this is graded Insufficient rather than Negative. A 1981 double-blind trial of oral zinc sulphate exists, but no abstract is available to report its results. In an uncontrolled 12-week study of 15 people with low blood zinc, 50 mg of zinc gluconate a day raised zinc levels; 9 of the 15 had some regrowth, which the authors reported was not statistically significant. A meta-analysis of 34 papers on blood trace elements found lower blood zinc in people with alopecia areata than in healthy controls; that is an association, not evidence that supplements help.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Zinc
general_safety.short: Nausea and bad taste were more common with zinc in common-cold trials. Case reports link zinc supplements and zinc overload to copper deficiency, causing anaemia or nerve damage.
